string.name: help_intro
string.translation_description: Help section: introduction and quick start. Please do not change the markup

resources.string:
Introduction and Quick Start

Hold your phone up and look through it like a window into space. Sky Map uses your phone\'s sensors to track where you\'re looking and update the star map in real time.

Not all phones are capable of running Sky Map! See the hardware requirements section below.

If this is your first time:

1. Allow location access when prompted — Sky Map needs your approximate location to draw the right sky for where you are.
2. Point your phone at the sky in any direction.
3. The map will move to match where you\'re looking.

string.name: help_navigating
string.translation_description: Help section: navigating the sky, automatic and manual modes. Please do not change the markup

resources.string:
Navigating the Sky

Tap the screen to bring up the controls and the head-up display (top right).

Automatic Mode

In Auto Mode (the default), Sky Map uses your phone\'s compass, accelerometer, and gyro sensors to show whatever is in the direction your phone is pointing. Just move your phone around and the map follows.

Use a two finger pinch to zoom in and out.

Manual Mode

With the controls visible, tap the hand button (bottom right) to switch to Manual Mode. In this mode you can:

• Drag the map with one finger to pan around.
• Pinch to zoom in or out.
• Rotate with two fingers to change orientation.
• Double tap the screen to toggle whether the horizon is kept horizontal as you drag.

Tap the compass button (bottom right) to switch back to Auto Mode.

string.name: help_layers
string.translation_description: Help section: the visible layers of the sky map. Please do not change the markup

resources.string:
Layers

Sky Map organizes what it shows into layers, each of which can be toggled on or off independently via the layer buttons on the left-hand side. Long press, or tap the Layers button near the bottom, to bring up toggles for more layers.


Current layers include:
• Stars: The brightest stars, with labels for notable ones
• Constellations: Constellation outlines and names
• Deep-sky objects: Galaxies, nebulae, star clusters, and other remarkable objects
• Solar system: The Sun, Moon, and planets, displayed as images
• Meteor showers: The radiant points of the annual meteor showers
• Celestial grid: The right-ascension / declination coordinate grid
• Ecliptic: The Sun\'s annual path through the sky, which the Moon and planets roughly follow
• Horizon: The horizon line and cardinal direction labels (N, S, E, W)
• Sky gradient: The daytime sky glow and twilight coloring near the horizon

The meteor shower radiants only show on the dates when the meteor showers are happening.

How big the planets are drawn

Tap the arrow beside Solar system in the Layers sheet to choose how the Sun, Moon and planets are sized:

• Glyphs (the default): big enough to see at any zoom, and sized by how big each body actually is rather than how big it looks from here — a model of the solar system rather than a view through a telescope. Saturn and its rings are the widest thing of all, then the Sun, then Jupiter, down to Pluto. The differences are squeezed to fit the screen: the Sun is really 586 times Pluto\'s width, not seven. The Moon is the exception, drawn the same size as the Sun, because that is how the two look from here.
• True scale: every body at its real size in the sky. The Sun and Moon are about half a degree across — roughly a pencil eraser held at arm\'s length — and the planets are specks until you zoom right in. Zoom all the way and Jupiter shows its belts, Saturn\'s rings separate from the planet, and an eclipse lines up exactly as it does in the sky.
• Steady: holds each body at a fixed size on the screen as you zoom, switching to the real size once you are zoomed in far enough for it to be the larger of the two.

The two modes tell you different things. Glyphs says Jupiter is a giant and Pluto is tiny. True scale says the Sun and Moon look almost exactly the same size from Earth — which is why a total solar eclipse works at all, and you can watch it happen.
Sky Map shows the geometric horizon — a perfectly flat, unobstructed view. Objects just above it may still be hidden by buildings, hills, or trees in practice.

string.name: help_info_cards
string.translation_description: Help section: the object info cards. Please do not change the markup

resources.string:
Info Cards

Tap a labeled celestial object on the sky map to bring up an info card — a panel with a photo and details about that object. Info cards are available for hundreds of objects including stars, planets, the Moon, notable deep-sky objects, and constellations.


Each card shows:

• A photograph or chart of the object
• A short description and a fun fact
• Scientific data such as distance, size, and object type

Tap the image inside the card to view it fullscreen. Dismiss the card by tapping outside it or pressing Back.

Not all objects have info cards, but we\'re adding more all the time.

string.name: help_search
string.translation_description: Help section: searching for objects in the sky. Please do not change the markup

resources.string:
Search

Tap the magnifier button (bottom) to search for anything in the sky.


You can search for:

• Stars — by name, e.g. \"Sirius\", \"Betelgeuse\", \"Polaris\"
• Planets — e.g. \"Mars\", \"Saturn\"
• Constellations — e.g. \"Orion\", \"Cassiopeia\"
• Deep-sky objects — e.g. \"M31\", \"Andromeda Galaxy\", \"Pleiades\"
• Coordinates — right ascension and declination, e.g. \"5h 55m, 7° 24\'\" (you can use an \'o\' for a degree symbol)

In Auto Mode: after selecting a result, Sky Map shows a targeting circle and a directional arrow. Follow the arrow by rotating your phone — the circle changes color as the object comes into your field of view. Tap Cancel (or press Back) to exit search.

In Manual Mode: the map simply jumps to center on the object.

You can search for objects that Sky Map doesn\'t show such as Europa, one of Jupiter\'s moons. In this case search will lead you to the parent object (Jupiter).

string.name: help_time_travel
string.translation_description: Help section: the time travel feature. Please do not change the markup

resources.string:
Time Travel

Time Travel lets you see the sky at any moment from the year 1600 to 3000. Tap the clock button (bottom).


Pick a popular event (eclipses, meteor-shower peaks, the next full or new moon, planet conjunctions, the Apollo 11 landing, and more) from the event list, set your own moment with the Set date and Set time buttons, or tap \"Start from now\" if you simply want to go forwards or backwards from the current moment.

Once in Time Travel mode, the date is shown on screen and playback controls let you move through time:

• Tap ▶▶ (faster) or ◀◀ (slower) to step the playback speed forward or backward through time
• Tap ❚❚ to pause
• Tap Now to jump back to the present

Some things you can use it for:

• What can I see just after sunset tonight?
• When is the next good chance to spot Mercury?
• What did the sky look like the night I was born?

Accuracy decreases for dates far from the present, mainly due to the gravitational influence of Jupiter.

string.name: help_night_vision
string.translation_description: Help section: night vision mode. Please do not change the markup

resources.string:
Night Vision Mode

If you\'re outside doing real observing, Night Vision mode helps preserve your dark-adapted eyesight. Toggle it with the Night Mode button at the bottom.


In Night Vision mode, Sky Map switches the display to deep red tones and dims the screen. The Auto screen dimming option in Settings gives you additional control over how dark the screen gets.

Other functions

Other functions can be found under the overflow menu (…) at the bottom right.

string.name: help_gallery
string.translation_description: Help section: the image gallery. Please do not change the markup

resources.string:
Gallery

The Gallery contains a curated collection of beautiful images of the night sky, including some from the Hubble Space Telescope.


Browse thumbnails by scrolling, and tap one to see details. Use the Find button to locate that object in the sky.

string.name: help_location
string.translation_description: Help section: setting your observing location. Please do not change the markup

resources.string:
Setting Your Location

Sky Map needs your approximate location to draw the correct sky. By default it uses your device\'s location services (mobile network or GPS).


If location access is unavailable or you\'d rather set it manually, tap the Enter Location Manually button and enter a place name or a latitude and longitude in degrees.

Internet is required to decode location place names.

If you\'ve previously denied Sky Map location permission, you may need to re-enable it in your device\'s App Settings → Permissions.

If you don\'t grant it access, Sky Map will assume you are at (0, 90) — the North Pole!

string.name: help_diagnostics
string.translation_description: Help section: the diagnostics page. Please do not change the markup

resources.string:
Diagnostics

This page lists various data about your phone and Sky Map that can be useful for debugging issues. Find it under Settings → Diagnostics.


When reporting a problem, tap the share button at the top of the page to email these details to us at skymapdevs@gmail.com. You can read and edit the report before sending it.

string.name: help_calibrate
string.translation_description: Help section: the calibrate page. Please do not change the markup

resources.string:
Calibrate

From time to time you should calibrate your phone\'s compass – this page shows you how. Sky Map will also warn you if your compass requires calibration.
IMPORTANT: A calibrated compass does NOT mean an accurate compass. All calibration does is reset the compass internally. It can still be inaccurate due to nearby magnetic interference or simply bad hardware. Almost all accuracy issues are due to the phone\'s hardware and are nothing to do with Sky Map. All Sky Map does is report to you what the phone is reporting to it.

See the troubleshooting section below for more help.

string.name: help_hardware
string.translation_description: Help section: hardware and sensor requirements. Please do not change the markup

resources.string:
Hardware Requirements

Not all devices can fully support Sky Map!


At the very least you need a phone with:

• A magnetic field sensor (aka a Compass) — to tell which direction you\'re facing
• An accelerometer — to tell how high up in the sky you\'re looking

Ideally also:

• A gyroscope — this will smooth out the motion and make it less jerky

Phone compasses are notoriously unreliable. If the sky map looks wrong, it is almost always a hardware issue with your phone\'s compass — not a bug in Sky Map. Sky Map reads exactly what your phone\'s sensor reports; it has no way to automatically correct a bad or biased reading. See Troubleshooting below.

How do I know which sensors my phone has?

Open Settings → Diagnostics — any sensors your phone doesn\'t have will be marked absent. You will also have been informed during the tutorial.

What if my device is missing required sensors?

Sky Map will fall back into manual mode. You can still explore the sky, but without the sensors there is no way any app can show you your direction.

string.name: help_troubleshooting
string.translation_description: Help section: troubleshooting a map that does not move or points the wrong way. Please do not change the markup

resources.string:
Troubleshooting

The map doesn\'t move

• Check you\'re in Auto Mode (not Manual)
• Check the Diagnostics page (Settings → Diagnostics) to confirm your device has a compass and accelerometer
• Try the figure-8 calibration gesture: wave your phone slowly in a large, smooth figure-8 shape

The map is pointing the wrong way or is inaccurate

Sky Map needs three things to show the correct sky: the direction your phone is facing, your location, and the current time. If the map looks wrong, one of these is likely off.

• Compass (most common cause): This is a hardware issue with your phone — not a Sky Map bug. The figure-8 calibration gesture asks your phone to reset its compass sensor internally, but a calibrated compass is not necessarily an accurate one. If you\'re near a metal object, car dashboard, or magnetic phone case the map can still be off even after calibrating. Move to an open area and repeat the figure-8 gesture.
• Location: Grant location permission via App Settings → Permissions. Check the Diagnostics page (Settings → Diagnostics) to confirm your coordinates. A telltale symptom of missing location is Polaris appearing directly overhead.
• Time: Less common, but an incorrect time zone shifts the whole sky. Check the Diagnostics page (Settings → Diagnostics) to confirm your device\'s time and time zone are correct.

The map is jittery

• If your phone has no gyroscope, turn on Use legacy sensors in sensor settings
• Adjust Sensor Speed and Damping under Settings → Sensor Settings (experts) (shown when Use legacy sensors is on)

For full troubleshooting details see the online troubleshooting guide.

If you\'re still stuck, email us at skymapdevs@gmail.com — a screenshot of your Diagnostics page is very helpful.

string.name: help_pointer_mode
string.translation_description: Help section: pointer mode for telescope users. Please do not change the markup

resources.string:
Telescope Users — Pointer Mode

Under Settings → Sensor Settings, change the View Direction to Pointer Mode. In this mode, Sky Map shows what the long edge of the phone is pointing at, rather than what the screen is facing.

This lets you mount your phone along the side of a telescope tube so the screen is perpendicular to the tube while the map still tracks what the telescope is aimed at.
